title: fetch() Basics
subtitle: Making GET requests, reading JSON responses, and handling the two-step promise
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Before fetch(), developers used XMLHttpRequest (XHR) — a verbose, callback-based API. jQuery's $.ajax() improved it but required a library dependency.
whyItExists.solution: The Fetch API is built into every modern browser. It returns Promises, works naturally with async/await, and has a clean, consistent interface. No library required.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any time you need to make HTTP requests from a browser or Node.js (18+, built-in). For complex cases (interceptors, request cancellation, progress), consider axios.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: When you need upload progress events in browsers (XHR has onprogress; fetch only supports download progress via ReadableStream). When targeting very old browsers (IE11 doesn't support fetch natively).

explainModes.beginner: fetch() makes a network request and returns a Promise. You await it to get the Response object. Then you call .json() (another Promise) to parse the body. Always check response.ok to know if the request succeeded — fetch() does NOT throw an error for 404 or 500 status codes, only for network failures.
explainModes.simple: const res = await fetch(url). res.ok: true if status 200-299. res.status: the HTTP status number. res.json(): Promise that parses body as JSON. res.text(): Promise that reads body as string. res.headers.get('content-type'): read a response header. fetch() only rejects on network failure (no internet, DNS error) — not on 4xx/5xx. You must check res.ok yourself. Common pattern: if (!res.ok) throw new Error(res.status).
explainModes.standard: Two-step Promise: fetch() resolves when headers are received (not body). response.json() / response.text() reads the body stream. This separation allows streaming large responses without loading them all into memory. Response body can only be read ONCE — calling .json() twice throws 'body already used'. Clone to read twice: const clone = res.clone(). AbortController: cancel a request — const ctrl = new AbortController(); fetch(url, { signal: ctrl.signal }); ctrl.abort(). Timeout pattern: AbortController + setTimeout.
explainModes.technical: Response object: url, status, statusText, ok, redirected, headers (Headers object), body (ReadableStream). Headers object: .get(name), .has(name), .entries(), .forEach(). request.headers vs response.headers: Request headers are what you send; Response headers are what the server returns. Content-Type negotiation: set Accept header to tell the server what format you want. Credential handling: fetch() by default sends no cookies. Add credentials: 'include' to send cookies (for same-origin) or credentials: 'include' with appropriate CORS headers for cross-origin.
explainModes.deepDive: Streaming responses: response.body is a ReadableStream. For large responses, use a reader: const reader = res.body.getReader(); while true { const { done, value } = await reader.read(); }. Useful for: server-sent events, large file downloads with progress, LLM streaming responses. Cache modes: fetch(url, { cache: 'no-cache' | 'no-store' | 'reload' | 'force-cache' | 'only-if-cached' }). Service Worker integration: fetch events can intercept all requests — the foundation of offline PWAs. node-fetch vs built-in fetch: Node 18+ includes a global fetch implementation based on undici. For older Node, use node-fetch or axios.

content.text: fetch() only rejects (throws) on network failure — not on 404 or 500 responses. Always check `if (!res.ok)` after awaiting, and throw manually if you want HTTP errors to be catchable.

questions.question: What does `response.ok` return when the server responds with a 404 status code?
options: true — the request was completed successfully
false — ok is true only for 2xx status codes (200-299)
undefined — ok only exists on successful responses
questions.explanation: response.ok is a shorthand for response.status >= 200 && response.status < 300. A 404 is a 4xx status, so ok is false. The fetch Promise itself still RESOLVES (doesn't throw) — you received a response, just not a successful one. This surprises many developers: you must check res.ok yourself if you want to treat HTTP errors as exceptions. fetch() only rejects for actual network failures (no connection, DNS failure, request aborted).

faq.q: Should I use fetch() or axios?
faq.a: fetch() is built-in and sufficient for most use cases. Use axios when you need: (1) automatic JSON serialization for request bodies (fetch requires JSON.stringify manually), (2) interceptors to add auth headers or handle errors globally, (3) request cancellation tokens (cleaner than AbortController), (4) upload progress events, (5) Node.js support < 18. For a browser-only app with simple needs, fetch() + a small wrapper function is the leaner choice.

examples: Next.js uses fetch() extended with caching options (next: { revalidate: 60 })
